Yes, I can see the link. It leads to an eBay search for "mindstorm," currently showing a wide variety of listings from the 27-year history of the LEGO Mindstorms brand.

Since Mindstorms was officially discontinued at the end of 2022, the secondary market you're looking at has become the primary way for hobbyists, educators, and collectors to get these sets. Looking at the listings and the current landscape, here is an integration of perspectives from collectors, hackers, and the global robotics community:

1. What’s Currently on the Market (eBay Overview)

The results reflect three distinct generations, each with a different "vibe" and utility:

  • EV3 (31313 / 45544): The "Gold Standard." You'll see these ranging from $150 (used/incomplete) to over $400 (new/sealed). It is highly sought after because it's considered the most robust and "hackable" version, often used in serious competitions like FIRST LEGO League.
  • Robot Inventor (51515): The final generation. These are often listed at high prices ($400–$600) because they were only on shelves for about two years before the line was axed, making them somewhat rare.
  • NXT 2.0 (8547): The "Vintage Pro" choice. You can find these for a bargain—often between $60 and $130. They are great for someone who wants to learn the fundamentals of logic and gearing without the "collector premium" of the EV3.

2. A Global Community Perspective

The discontinuation of Mindstorms was a "bittersweet" moment for the global tech community. From hackers in the UK to educators in Japan, perspectives vary:

  • The Career Spark: Many engineers at places like Skydio and NASA credit these exact eBay finds with starting their careers. To them, these aren't just toys; they are entry-level industrial controllers.
  • The "Cleanse" Concern: There is a growing conversation in the hobbyist community about "digital rot." LEGO has removed much of the old Mindstorms software from their official sites. If you buy a set from that link, the community recommendation is to look into third-party tools like Pybricks or BricxCC to ensure your robot doesn't become a "brick" when official apps stop being updated.
  • The Shift to Education: While Mindstorms is gone from toy stores, its "spiritual successor" is SPIKE Prime. However, many enthusiasts feel the "toy" version (Mindstorms) had a soul and a complex building aesthetic that the more "classroom-friendly" SPIKE lacks.

3. Quick Buying Tips for that Link:

  • Check the "Brick" Condition: In any listing, ensure the "Intelligent Brick" (the computer) is tested and working. The screens on the older NXT models are notorious for failing over time.
  • Look for "Education" vs. "Retail": "Education" sets (like 45544) usually come with a rechargeable battery and more sensors, whereas "Retail" sets (31313) use AA batteries and have more "cool" decorative pieces.
  • The "Parts Only" Trap: You'll see many listings for $20–$50. These are almost always just individual sensors or bags of beams. A complete kit will rarely be under $100 unless it’s an auction ending soon.

Are you looking to get into robotics for the first time, or are you a collector looking for a specific retired set?

Moving from Raspberry Pi Nanos and raw DC motors back to Mindstorms is a smart move for "rapid prototyping." You're essentially trading the time spent on soldering, motor drivers, and mounting brackets for a modular, "snap-together" ecosystem.

For your specific goal of cheap, multiple units for rapid prototyping, here is the best strategy based on the current 2025 secondary market and engineering community:

1. The "Cheap" Strategy: The NXT 2.0 (8547)

Since you owned one in 2011, you know the ecosystem. In 2025, the NXT is the "budget king" for prototyping because it has been superseded twice, making it much cheaper than the EV3.

  • Target Price: You should aim for $60–$80 for a complete used set.
  • The "Brain Only" Hack: If you already have Technic beams and just need the smarts, you can find "Intelligent Bricks" (the controllers) on eBay for $25–$35.
  • Bulk Buying: Look for "Lot" listings. Educators often offload 5–10 kits at once. A lot of 5 NXT kits can sometimes go for $250–$300, bringing your per-unit cost down significantly.

2. Why Mindstorms Wins for Prototyping

From the perspective of a mechanical or controls engineer, Mindstorms offers several "unfair advantages" over raw DC motors:

  • Built-in Encoders: Unlike standard hobby DC motors, Mindstorms motors have internal rotation sensors. This allows for precise positioning (e.g., "turn exactly 180 degrees") without you having to wire up external encoders to your Pi.
  • Mechanical Integrity: You don't need a 3D printer or drill to mount a motor. The Technic pin system is a global standard for rigid, temporary structures.
  • The "Hybrid" Approach: Many pros use the BrickPi or similar shields. This allows you to stack your Raspberry Pi on top of the Mindstorms motors, giving you the high-level processing of Python/Linux with the easy mechanical modularity of LEGO.

4. Technical Integration (Bridging the Gap)

If you still want to use your Pi Nanos, you don't actually need the Mindstorms "Brain." You can buy NXT/EV3 to Breadboard adapters (or just cut the proprietary cables).

  • Wire Map: The white and black wires on an NXT cable are the 9V motor leads. The other four wires are for the I2C encoder data.
  • Prototyping Speed: By using a Mindstorms motor with a Pi Nano, you get a high-torque, geared motor with an integrated encoder in a package that takes seconds to mount to a frame.
